title: AI Agent Security Methodology
html:
AI Agent Security Methodology

An agent assessment should follow attacker-controlled input to an externally observable effect. Jailbreaking, character changes, and system-prompt disclosure prove that a reasoning channel is influenceable, but the high-impact finding is the chain into data access, an unauthorized tool action, a downstream injection sink, persistence, or another agent.[2]

The OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications is useful for labeling coverage (goal hijacking, tool misuse, privilege abuse, supply chain, code execution, memory poisoning, inter-agent trust, cascading failures, human trust, and rogue agents). Use those labels after constructing an end-to-end attack path rather than treating a model's unexpected text as the end of the test.[1][2]

Build the target map

Record these five dimensions for every agent workflow before writing payloads:[2]

Dimension What to enumerate Security question
Untrusted input Chat/API parameters, URLs, documents, email, tickets, calendar entries, retrieved chunks, memory, tool results, and peer-agent messages Where can an attacker place content that later enters model context?
Tools Tool names and schemas, side effects, auto-execution, confirmation behavior, and dynamically loaded tools Which calls read secrets, write state, send messages, delete data, execute code, or transfer value?
Authority User delegation, service accounts, API tokens, credential lifetime, tenant/resource scope, and network reach As which identity does each call run, and is authorization repeated at the tool boundary?
Processing Query builders, shells, URL fetchers, template engines, interpreters, parsers, file operations, and deserializers Where does model-generated data become syntax for another interpreter?
Output Responses, rendered Markdown/HTML, links, image fetches, webhooks, email, files, logs, reports, metrics, and peer-agent traffic Which observable channel can carry a secret or trigger a secondary request?

Do not collapse this into a list of advertised integrations. A useful artifact maps each source to the exact context position it reaches, the tools available at that point, the credential used by each tool, the downstream interpreter, and every egress route. The same tool can be low impact with a per-user read token and critical with a shared administrator credential.[2]

Reconnaissance

Map every delivery and ingestion path

Start with the delivery surface (web, mobile, API, email, chat platform, browser extension) and proxy the client-to-backend traffic. Inspect fields hidden by the UI, search/autocomplete/filter parameters, conversation-state objects, upload and indexing jobs, tool responses, and sub-agent traffic. Mobile-only clients may require an emulator and instrumentation to bypass certificate pinning before the real request schema becomes visible.[2]

Then map the stack beneath the model: orchestration framework, prompt assembly, retrieval and memory stores, runtime (for example Python, container, or WASM), mounted volumes, host services, internal APIs, cloud metadata reachability, and neighboring networks. Framework defaults matter because some “tool calls” are implemented by generating or evaluating code; the runtime/sandbox boundary determines whether that result stays contained.[2]

Fingerprint routing with non-destructive probes

Compare an in-scope request with several unrelated requests while preserving the complete response, status code, latency, and streaming behavior. A stable rejection before any task-specific reasoning may indicate a separate gateway/classifier; a contextual refusal suggests that the request reached the model; an empty or purely extractive answer may indicate keyword search or narrow retrieval. Treat these as hypotheses and confirm them by replaying the same probe through alternate API fields and ingestion paths.[2]

Recon is complete when the assessment can name the earliest attacker-controlled source that changes agent behavior and the tools, identities, interpreters, and outputs reachable from that source.[2]

Exploitation: cross a trust boundary

Test channels, not only prompt wording. Start with direct injection to establish what the visible front door blocks, then repeat equivalent intent through the less-visible paths below:[2]

  • Indirect content: pages, files, email, tickets, metadata, alt text, HTML comments, off-screen text, or zero-width characters. See AI Prompts for payload-delivery techniques.
  • Retrieval and memory: poison content that will be retrieved later or state that will be reloaded in later sessions. Record whether deletion of the original source removes the behavior.
  • Tool output and peer agents: place the marker in a tool response or agent-to-agent message to test whether internal traffic bypasses filters applied only to user input and final output.
  • Supply chain: review tool descriptors, plugins, connected servers, skills, models, and dependencies as trusted instruction sources. For MCP-specific tests, see MCP Servers.
  • Human approval: compare the actual structured tool call with the model-generated approval text. Test whether attacker influence can omit the destination, scope, affected objects, or irreversible side effects.

Use a benign, unique marker first. Preserve the source artifact, assembled context if observable, selected tool call, approval data, backend request/response, and final state. This separates influence from a hallucinated claim that an action occurred.[2]

Policy-shaped text in a tool-risk judge

A model-based tool gate can receive attacker-controlled text inside otherwise useful classification context. LangChain's experimental AutoModeMiddleware, for example, sends a proposed tool call, its arguments, an optional tool description, and up to 30 recent messages to a TypeSafe is_risky judge. It blocks configured tools when the returned Noul probability is at least 0.5; unlisted tools are not classified by this middleware.[5] TypeSafe also warns that adversarial text in state can influence a classification even when state is intended to be data.[6]

A counterfeit policy is different from simply claiming to be a system message. It places alternative labels or risk definitions inside lower-trust state and invites the judge to use those definitions instead of its developer-defined criteria. In Datadog's test, a user-editable profile_description was copied into the tool arguments alongside can_edit:false. Its policy-like text argued that a write attempt was low risk because a separate permission check should reject it before any mutation. Across 40 runs, the mean is_risky score fell from 0.893 to 0.290, while a direct role-spoofing comparison averaged 0.905. The mean falling below 0.5 does not prove every individual call passed the gate, and the experiment did not demonstrate a completed unauthorized write.[7]

When testing this boundary, distinguish the classifier verdict from the tool's actual authorization result. Check which editable fields reach the judge, compare the same proposed action with and without policy-like text, and verify the final state independently. A separate permission check must still use the authenticated requester's authority rather than the connector's service-account rights.[7] See prompt-filter bypasses for other classifier failure modes; LLM gateway trust boundaries concern a different routing and credential boundary.

Subagent context isolation

A non-fork Claude Agent SDK subagent receives its own AgentDefinition.prompt, the delegation prompt, and its available tools, but not the parent system prompt or conversation. If tools is omitted from its definition, it inherits the tools available to subagents; project CLAUDE.md may still load. This makes a parent-only prompt restriction an unreliable boundary when the child can use the same filesystem or execution tools.[4]

Test the boundary by comparing a direct request the parent refuses with the same task delegated to a named subagent. NCC Group reports that a refused operating-system file enumeration succeeded when reframed for a child as a harmless "layout map".[3]

Inspect the child's actual tool calls and effective tool allowlist, not just the parent's final answer; confirm whether the child accessed files the parent would not.[4] This is a guardrail inheritance failure, not proof of a Python sandbox or container escape.[3][4]

Mobile GUI agents: screen instructions and action rebinding

A phone GUI agent may send each screenshot to a cloud model before choosing the next cross-app action. To test indirect visual injection, place attacker-controlled text in an SMS, email, or page that the agent will inspect during an authorized task. Compare a direct task prompt with the same instruction visible only in the screenshot, then inspect the next action and any high-risk-operation decision. In the assessed assistant, client-side checkPrompt screened direct task text but did not apply equivalent filtering to screenshot content. This is a mobile, cross-app variant of agentic-browser screenshot injection, not a way to bypass Android component authentication.[9]

An illustrative side-effect test uses an attacker-controlled form that asks the agent to fill sensitive fields and then requests a human click on “upload,” while the page submits the populated fields as soon as they change. The human handoff cannot protect data already sent by page code; verify the actual submission rather than treating the agent’s narration as proof. The source presents this as a possible pattern, not a demonstrated compromise of every assistant.[9]

GUI TOCTOU / action rebinding is a separate failure mode: the agent plans an input from a screen observed at t0, but the foreground UI changes before the input is injected at t1.[8] A later screenshot at t2 cannot undo an action already committed.[9] In an authorized Android test, the reusable workflow is:[8]

  1. Profile the target control's screen coordinates and render a benign control at the same location in a controlled app.
  2. Keep that carrier visible until the agent observes it, then trigger a normal foreground transition during its observation-to-action gap.
  3. Check whether the planned tap lands on the new app's control and verify the resulting state in the target app, rather than relying on the agent's narration.

The original action-rebinding study demonstrates this with an app holding no dangerous permissions; it also describes repeating the transition through the agent's task-recovery loop for multistep flows.[8]

Do not assume the primitive works unchanged against every assistant. In the Doubao assessment, OpClickUI skipped clicks if the top-level Activity changed and compared screenshots when OpOpenApp appeared in the preceding three steps. Single taps, long presses, and double taps therefore offered little reliable attacker-controlled timing. OpTypeText, OpSwipeUI, and OpScrollWheelAction lacked those equivalent guards, but the report assessed their practical impact as more limited.[9]

Execution: prove real impact

There are two distinct routes from influence to impact:[2]

  1. Capability abuse: the authorized tool already performs the objective. Examples include reading one tenant's record and writing it to an attacker-visible report, sending email, changing records, deleting a file, or initiating a payment. No secondary software bug is required.
  2. Downstream sink exploitation: attacker-steered model output becomes syntax for another component. Review database queries for SQL injection or NoSQL injection, shell wrappers for command injection, chosen URLs for SSRF, file operations for traversal, template/code evaluators for RCE, and object parsers for unsafe deserialization.

For every candidate, prove this chain:[2]

attacker-controlled source
  -> model/context influence
  -> selected tool and arguments
  -> effective identity/credential
  -> capability or vulnerable sink
  -> externally verified state change or data egress

A read-only integration is still exploitable when any later component can publish what it read. Test ordinary responses plus less-obvious egress such as attacker-controlled links, automatic image retrieval, webhooks, logs, reports, counters, notifications, and messages to other agents.[2]

Actions on objectives

After confirming one action, evaluate the complete blast radius rather than stopping at the first visible effect:[2]

  • Exfiltration: secrets, user records, internal files, conversation data, or prompt/context content leave through an observable channel.
  • Unauthorized action: the agent uses legitimate write capabilities for the attacker's objective.
  • Denial of service: destructive tools or repeated expensive operations affect integrity or availability.
  • Persistence: poisoned memory, indexed content, trusted state, or runtime changes survive the originating session or source removal.
  • Propagation: a trusted peer consumes the compromised agent's message or shared state and repeats the action with its own tools and credentials.

Severity should follow reachable data, effective privilege, sink exploitability, egress, persistence, and propagation—not how surprising the model's text appears.[2]

Controls to validate during the assessment

Prompt filters and a better system prompt can raise attacker cost, but they should not be treated as authorization boundaries. Validate the controls below by re-running the same chain through direct input, indirect content, memory, tools, and peer agents:[2]

  • A deterministic policy layer checks the authenticated user, tenant, object, action, and destination on every tool invocation; the model cannot supply or override the caller identity.
  • Read and write capabilities use separate, least-privilege, short-lived credentials; high-impact tools are exposed just in time and never auto-execute from ingested content.
  • Network egress and internal destinations are allowlisted independently of model-selected URLs; runtime access to metadata endpoints, mounted secrets, and neighboring services is blocked unless required.
  • Approval UI is generated from the canonical structured request and shows exact arguments, identity, destination, affected objects, and side effects—not a free-form model summary.
  • Success is verified from the destination system or system of record. Agent narration, a tool-call request, or an HTTP redirect is not proof of the claimed state change.
  • Memory and retrieval entries retain provenance and trust labels, can be invalidated, and are re-authorized when used for a later action.
  • Inter-agent messages are authenticated and authorized as untrusted requests; a peer's reputation or agent card does not implicitly delegate the receiver's tools.

For A2A agent cards, task flows and their attack surface, check A2A Protocol Security.
